points_of_disagreement: Whether the 2026 election represents genuine democratic choice or a managed mandate-seeking exercise by an entrenched incumbent
Whether Pérez's 5% stake sale plan represents the first step toward dismantling member ownership or a legitimate modernization strategy
Whether the two-season trophy drought is an unprecedented sporting failure or a temporary setback within a historically successful tenure
Whether campaign promises (Klopp, Haaland, €150m signings) were credible commitments or populist tactics designed to manipulate voters
Whether Anas Laghrari's informal influence represents a governance deficit or effective advisory support
Whether the 20-year membership and 15% budget guarantee requirements are structural barriers that entrench incumbents or legitimate safeguards for institutional stability
Whether restoring Spanish player development and La Fábrica should be a presidential priority or whether global recruitment is the correct strategy
Whether the absence of Real Madrid players from Spain's World Cup squad reflects institutional decline or reflects broader changes in Spanish football talent distribution
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that Real Madrid held a contested 2026 presidential election between Pérez and Riquelme—the first contested election in 20 years—following a two-season trophy drought, with Pérez having announced a 5% stake sale plan and both candidates making transfer/managerial campaign pledges. The disagreement centers on whether this election signals democratic renewal or managed entrenchment, whether the trophy drought and privatization plan represent genuine institutional failure, and whether campaign promises were credible or populist theater.

framings.name: Democratic Renewal & Historic Milestone
framings.question: Does this election represent a meaningful restoration of democratic accountability at one of the world's most powerful sports institutions?
framings.key_claim: After 20 years of uncontested elections, Real Madrid's socios are finally exercising genuine democratic choice, marking a historic inflection point for the club's governance.
framings.description: This framing treats the mere existence of a contested election as the story, emphasizing the rarity and civic significance of members having a real vote for the first time since 2006. It foregrounds participation, process legitimacy, and the health of the member-owned model.
framings.emphasizes: Voter turnout, the 20-year gap since the last contested election, the procedural legitimacy of the Electoral Board, and the symbolic weight of socios exercising their franchise.
framings.downplays: The structural barriers to candidacy (20-year membership requirement, 15% budget guarantee) that make genuine competition rare; the likelihood that the incumbent wins easily.

Real Madrid returns to the polls after 20 years with the duel between Florentino Pérez and Enrique Riquelme

framings.name: Ownership & Privatization Threat
framings.question: Is the member-owned identity of Real Madrid at existential risk, and is this election the last chance to stop privatization?
framings.key_claim: Florentino Pérez's plan to sell a 5% stake to a private investor is the first step toward dismantling the member-owned model that defines Real Madrid's identity.
framings.description: This framing, primarily driven by the Riquelme campaign and amplified by soccer media, casts the election as a referendum on whether Real Madrid will remain a socio-owned institution or drift toward the investor-owned Premier League model. It treats the 5% stake sale as a Trojan horse.
framings.emphasizes: Pérez's confirmed plan to sell a 5% stake, the precedent set by Premier League privatizations, the erosion of socio voting power, and Riquelme's warnings about 'the last election.'
framings.downplays: Pérez's counter-argument that the stake sale is merely a valuation mechanism and would legally entrench socio ownership; the fact that 5% is a minority stake with no governance rights.

framings.name: Sporting Accountability & Trophy Drought
framings.question: Has Florentino Pérez's leadership failed on the pitch, and should a trophyless era trigger a change at the top?
framings.key_claim: Back-to-back seasons without a single major trophy — an unprecedented drought since 2008–2010 — expose a sporting failure that Pérez's re-election bid cannot paper over with transfer promises.
framings.description: This framing evaluates the election through the lens of on-field results, arguing that the trophy drought is the proximate cause of the election being called and the primary metric by which Pérez's presidency should be judged. It scrutinizes whether Galáctico signings and managerial appointments are genuine sporting strategy or electoral theater.
framings.emphasizes: The two-season trophy drought, the unprecedented nature of the slump, Pérez's €150m signing promise and Mourinho announcement as campaign tactics, and Riquelme's charge that Super League obsession distracted from sporting priorities.
framings.downplays: Pérez's broader legacy of Champions League titles and the Bernabéu renovation; the argument that one bad cycle does not define a presidency.

framings.name: Campaign Credibility & Populist Promises
framings.question: Are the candidates' headline pledges — Haaland, Klopp, Mourinho, €150m signings — credible sporting plans or cynical electioneering?
framings.key_claim: Both candidates made spectacular, largely unverifiable transfer and managerial promises during the campaign, with Riquelme's Klopp and Haaland pledges publicly rejected by the players' own representatives before voting day.
framings.description: This framing scrutinizes the credibility and feasibility of campaign promises, treating the election as a spectacle of competitive populism. It highlights the gap between campaign rhetoric and reality — Klopp's agent flatly denied interest, Haaland's camp laughed off the claims, and Manchester City threatened legal action.
framings.emphasizes: Klopp's agent's public rejection, Manchester City's legal threat over Haaland's name being used, the notarized Haaland/Rodri guarantee, and Pérez's unnamed €150m 'Galáctico' tease.
framings.downplays: The possibility that some promises (e.g., Mourinho, Konaté) were genuine and pre-agreed; the tradition of bold electoral pledges in Spanish football (Pérez's Figo promise in 2000).

framings.name: Institutional Power & Governance Opacity
framings.question: Does Florentino Pérez's inner circle exercise unaccountable power over the club's most consequential decisions, and does the election expose structural governance failures?
framings.key_claim: The concentration of decision-making power around Pérez and unelected associates like Anas Laghrari — who has no official club position yet shapes Super League strategy and privatization plans — represents a governance deficit that the election has finally forced into the open.
framings.description: This framing focuses on who actually runs Real Madrid behind the scenes, questioning the transparency of major decisions (Super League, privatization, transfer policy) and the accountability of informal power brokers. It treats the election as a rare moment of institutional scrutiny.
framings.emphasizes: Anas Laghrari's informal influence, Pérez's refusal to debate Riquelme on television, the absence of a formal sporting director, and the opacity of the 5% stake sale process.
framings.downplays: The argument that concentrated executive authority is common and effective in elite football clubs; Pérez's track record of successful institutional outcomes.

framings.name: Continuity, Legacy & Institutional Stability
framings.question: Does Florentino Pérez's record of trophies, the Bernabéu renovation, and financial modernization justify continued leadership, and is the challenger a credible alternative?
framings.key_claim: Florentino Pérez's unmatched record of Champions League titles, the new Bernabéu, and financial stability makes him the only credible steward of Real Madrid's future, and the election is a mandate-seeking exercise rather than a genuine contest.
framings.description: This framing, largely carried by Pérez's campaign and sympathetic institutional voices, presents the election as a referendum on a successful presidency rather than a genuine competition. It foregrounds legacy, institutional continuity, and the challenger's inexperience.
framings.emphasizes: Pérez's Champions League record, the Bernabéu renovation, the Bernabéu Infinito/Apple partnership, confirmed signings (Konaté, Dumfries, Mourinho), and the challenger's lack of institutional experience.
framings.downplays: The trophy drought, governance opacity concerns, the 5% stake controversy, and the structural barriers that have kept elections uncontested for 20 years.

framings.name: Spanish Identity & Cultural Nationalism
framings.question: Has Real Madrid drifted away from its Spanish roots, and should the club's presidency be used to reassert a distinctly Spanish sporting and cultural identity?
framings.key_claim: With Spain naming a World Cup squad containing no Real Madrid players for the first time in history, the club has lost its role as the backbone of La Roja, and restoring that identity should be a presidential priority.
framings.description: This framing, originating with Riquelme, treats the election as a contest over the club's cultural soul — its relationship to Spanish football, the national team, and the peñas tradition — rather than purely a financial or sporting governance question.
framings.emphasizes: The historic absence of Real Madrid players from Spain's World Cup squad, Riquelme's pledge to revive La Fábrica and Spanish player development, the restoration of the Bernabéu Trophy and peñas relationships.
framings.downplays: The global commercial logic that drives modern elite clubs toward international rosters; the argument that nationality-based squad building may conflict with sporting merit.
sample_headlines: Riquelme pledges to revive Real Madrid's Spanish identity and restore club as key feeder for La Roja

framings.name: Structural Barriers & Incumbent Entrenchment
framings.question: Do Real Madrid's candidacy rules — 20-year membership, 15% budget guarantee — make genuine democratic competition structurally impossible, regardless of who wins?
framings.key_claim: The strict eligibility requirements that have kept Pérez's last five re-elections uncontested reveal that Real Madrid's democratic model is structurally designed to entrench incumbents, making this election an exception that proves the rule.
framings.description: This framing, carried primarily by analytical and prediction-market commentary, steps back from the candidates to question whether the club's governance rules permit meaningful democratic competition at all. It treats the 20-year gap between contested elections as a structural symptom, not an accident.
framings.emphasizes: The 20-year membership requirement, the 15% annual budget guarantee as a financial barrier, five consecutive uncontested re-elections, and the rarity of a challenger meeting the threshold.
framings.downplays: The argument that these rules protect the club from opportunistic or underqualified candidates; the fact that a challenger did emerge and was validated this cycle.

gap_analysis: Missing framings include: (1) Economic/Financial Management—how candidates differ on debt, wage structure, or commercial strategy; (2) Fan Experience & Stadium Culture—perspectives on matchday operations, ticket pricing, or supporter engagement; (3) Women's Football & Competitive Expansion—the role of Real Madrid Femenino or youth academy investment in candidate platforms; (4) International vs. Local Representation—whether candidates emphasize global commercial reach or Spanish/European roots differently; (5) Generational Divide—how younger vs. older members view modernization, social media presence, or player recruitment philosophy.
